blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews Tony Hoare's 1981 ACM Turing Award lecture, which serves as a powerful critique of overambitious software design and committee-driven language standardization. The paper emphasizes the pursuit of simplicity as the key to reliability, contrasting two approaches to software design: making systems so simple that deficiencies are obvious, or so complex that deficiencies are hidden. Hoare shares personal experiences from his work on ALGOL, PL/I, and Ada, highlighting the dangers of committee-based design and the importance of static type checking and safety-first principles. He argues that reliability cannot be achieved without simplicity, and that overambition often leads to failure despite the best intentions of intelligent programmers. The lecture also recounts the invention of QuickSort and the axiomatic approach to programming, offering timeless lessons on humility and the limits of ambition in software engineering.
paper_venue: ACM Turing Award Lecture, published in CACM
